content.text: An interface is a CONTRACT. Like a job description: "You MUST be able to code in Java, write tests, and do code reviews." It doesn't tell you HOW — just WHAT is required. Any class that signs the contract (implements) MUST fulfill every requirement. An abstract class is a PARTIAL blueprint — some rooms are built, some are left empty for you to finish.

content.annotation: Abstract = "I provide the skeleton, you fill in the details." Children are FORCED to implement abstract methods — compile error if they don't. This guarantees every test has a runTest() method.

content.modification: Bicycle implements Drivable but only defines start(), not stop().
content.question: What happens?
options: Compile error — must implement ALL interface methods
content.explanation: Interfaces are a CONTRACT. If you sign it (implements), you MUST fulfill EVERY method. Missing even ONE = compile error. This is how Java enforces that every implementor has the required capabilities.

content.label: Abstract Class vs Interface — when to use which?
content.question: Key difference?
options: Abstract can have fields + constructors. Interface cannot.
content.explanation: Abstract classes have: fields, constructors, both abstract AND concrete methods. Interfaces have: only method signatures + default methods (since Java 8), NO fields (only constants), NO constructors. Use abstract when sharing STATE. Use interface when sharing BEHAVIOR contracts.

content.annotation: Default methods let interfaces provide shared logic WITHOUT forcing an abstract class. Implementors get the behavior for free but can override if needed. This is how modern Java frameworks provide functionality without deep inheritance trees.

content.modification: Class C implements two interfaces with the same default method.
content.question: What happens?
options: Compile error — must override to resolve conflict
content.explanation: Diamond problem! When two interfaces have the same default method, the implementing class MUST override it to resolve the ambiguity. Java won't guess which one you want.

content.prompt: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?
options: When you need shared state (fields) and partial implementation
When a class needs to implement multiple contracts
When you want unrelated classes to share behavior
When you only need method signatures with no body
